$comment: Riftlight authored opening draft. Development preview only; see ../README.md. Production campaign id will be riftlight. No bonus XP: preserve the design bible campaign budget.
title: Snow on the Quay

goal.text: Find out where the snow on the quay is coming from.

steps.label: Find where the cold comes from

market.narration: The Exchange has put its market stalls back along the quay. Fish slap in buckets. A noodle seller lifts her awning with a broom. You have come back from the mountain, and three different people wave before you reach the water. Then a snowflake lands in your breakfast. The sky is clear, and snow should not be falling at all. Today's job is simple: find out where this snow is coming from. The noodle seller waves her broom at you. "Find your snow in a minute! First I need hands. This awning is heavy, and I pay in coins."

choices.label: Lend a hand with the awning

awning_plan.narration: Snow is piling up on the awning. It sags in the middle like a hammock, and the poles wobble. Under it, the noodle pot steams up at the sky. "Quick!" says the noodle seller. "Before it all lands in my broth!" How will you save the awning? Somebody's hat has blown off, and nobody has gone after it. The hat looks hurt.

choices.label: Tie the corners to the stall rail
Use brace to plant the middle pole

awning_lift.prompt: Everyone takes a pole! Lift the awning together on the noodle seller's count: one, two, UP! The snow on top is heavier than it looks.

awning_tie.prompt: Grab a corner rope and tie it to the stall rail before the next gust. Fast fingers win.

awning_brace.prompt: Brace holds the middle pole steady. Can you haul the sagging cloth tight around it?

awning_up.narration: The awning snaps tight. The snow slides off in one long whoosh and lands on a startled crate. The noodle seller bows with her broom. "Three coins, as promised," she says, and drops them in your hands. Then she wraps up a supper bundle: flatbread, cheese and a sausage. "For later. Don't tell the pot. The pot thinks everything here is for the pot." The sausage looks rather proud of itself. Somewhere up the quay, a tiny cheer goes up for no reason at all.

awning_flap.narration: The awning flaps like a huge wet bird. A pole clangs, and a pot of broth tips into the gutter. The noodle seller catches the cloth just in time and ties it down herself, muttering at it. "That is for trying," she says, and presses one coin into your hand. "The broth is for the gutter. The gutter is very pleased." The pot, half empty now, gurgles in a hurt way.

noodle_counter.narration: Her stall smells of ginger and warm honey. The honeycakes cool on their rack, steaming a little, as if they were thinking. "Honeycake is three coins," says the noodle seller. "Questions are free. Go and look at the fish stall, the gull on the post and that ship. They are all wrong this morning, and not one of them is sorry." Behind her, the snow keeps falling on nobody in particular. From the next stall, somebody sings about onions, off key and entirely happy.

choices.label: Go and look at the strange things

noodle_buy.narration: She slides a honeycake into a paper twist and counts your coins twice, just to enjoy it. "Eat it warm," she says, "or save it for somebody who needs it more than you do." A snowflake lands on the cake and gives up at once.

choices.label: Go and look at the strange things

morning.narration: Snow falls over one fish stall. The sky above it is clear. On a mooring post, a gull shakes frost from its wings. Beyond it, a ship has docked a day early. Its kitsune captain is arguing with the harbor clock. Where do you look first?

choices.label: Look at the snowy fish stall
Talk to the early ship captain

fish.narration: The fish seller holds up a scoop of snow. "I ordered ice. Ice stays where you put it." Snow lands in the scoop. Under her table, a patch of pebbles and stiff white grass has pushed up between the boards. It is cold enough to sting your fingers. She waves at her buckets. "Somebody move these, before my fish catch cold!"

choices.label: Move the fish out of the snow
Follow the trail of white grass

fish_buckets.prompt: Every bucket needs a pair of hands! Pass them down the line, out of the snow and under the awning, before the fish catch cold.

fish_help.narration: You pass the buckets down the line and tuck them under the noodle awning. Every fish stays wet and none stay cold. The fish seller wraps a dry cloth around your fingers, then presses two coins into your palm. "Something else stepped off that patch of grass," she says. "Little hooves. Went that way." She points along the quay, where wet hoofprints trail between stacks of crates.

fish_slosh.narration: The line wobbles. A bucket tips, and fish flop across the boards in a silver wave. Everyone chases them with nets, hats and one noodle ladle. At last every fish is back in water, and everyone is wet. The fish seller counts twice. "Nobody lost a fish," she says, "but I lost count of twelve." She tucks a coin into your hand. "Something else stepped off that patch of grass. Little hooves. Went that way." She points along the quay, where wet hoofprints trail between stacks of crates.

gull.narration: The gull stands on one foot. "Cold," it says. It changes feet. "Still cold." You ask where it has been. It points its beak toward the far end of the quay. "Here! I was here the whole time!" Its stomach growls. "That is the wind," it says. "Not my stomach." A small white hoofprint marks the boards below it.

choices.label: Let it warm its feet on a sleeve
Share a bite of your supper with the gull

gull_help.narration: The gull settles on your sleeve, tucking its icy feet into the fold. "For the record," it says, "I did not ask to become a winter bird." From your arm, it spots more hoofprints between the crates and calls them out.

gull_fed.narration: The gull swallows the crumbs and goes very still. "That," it says, "was the best thing that has happened to me today." It fluffs up until it is twice its size. Warm at last, it flaps to the top of a crate and points with its beak. "Hoofprints! Little ones! That way!" Then it adds, quieter, "Thank you. Don't tell the other gulls I said so."

ship.narration: The captain spreads a route chart over a barrel. "Our island was here yesterday." She taps a mark. "This morning the dock was over there. Same island. Same laundry on the line. Wrong patch of sky." She catches the chart by one corner before the wind takes it. "Captain Thimble. If you find a sensible explanation, save me a copy."

choices.label: Help her pin the chart down
Ask about the cold on the quay

chart_pin.prompt: The wind grabs the chart! Pin down the corners before it sails into the harbor.

ship_help.narration: You hold the corners while Captain Thimble ties the chart to the barrel. She gives you a quick, grateful nod and digs in her coat. "Spare ship's whistle. It's loud enough to wake a whale. If you ever need a hand in a hurry, blow it." She presses the brave whistle into your palm. "Look for me if you reach the islands. You will recognize the washing." A gust lifts the smell of snow from the far end of the quay.

ship_flap.narration: The chart tears loose and flaps across the quay like an enormous pale bird. Captain Thimble chases it past three crates and a bucket, then dives and sits on it. "Never," she says, out of breath, "trust a map on a windy day." She tucks it under her arm. "Look for me if you reach the islands. You will recognize the washing." A gust lifts the smell of snow from the far end of the quay.

ship_cold.narration: "There." The captain points past the noodle stall. "The wind is coming from between those crates. Wind should have more room than that." A coil of rope begins sliding across the wet boards toward them. Captain Thimble stamps on the end of it. The rope stops, and sulks.

trail_check.prompt: Snow, frost and small hoofprints all lead the same way along the quay, and fresh flakes are covering them. Can you tell which marks are newest? Small hooves, four to a set.

trail_found.narration: The newest marks are crisp, with a puff of white fuzz stuck in one. They run toward the far end of the quay, then skid sideways, as if their owner had been tugged and had not liked it. You follow them past a row of barrels. Then a deep horn blows from the water. Each print is no bigger than a plum, with a little frost around its edge.

choices.label: See what the horn is for

trail_lost.narration: Snow covers the marks before you can read them. You lose the trail among the barrels and end up with a boot full of slush. Then a deep horn blows from the water. You will have to find those little hooves another way. A barrel rolls a short way by itself, thinks better of it, and stops.

choices.label: See what the horn is for

delivery.narration: The barge bumps the quay hard enough to rattle the barrels. The pilot points at a flight of stone landing steps hanging crooked above the water. "Those were under my feet this morning. Now my regular landing is halfway up a wall." Sacks of potatoes slide across his deck. "That is supper for six boats. Help me get it ashore!" His webbed hands wave in two directions at once.

choices.label: Find the barge a safe place to tie up
Use rally to set a pace for the sack line
Carry the barge's rope up on wings

sack_line.prompt: Make a line along the planks and pass the sacks hand to hand. Everyone has to keep the same pace, or the potatoes will pile up! The pilot counts the sacks in a worried voice: nine, ten, ten, eleven.

sack_rally.prompt: A songkeeper's rally sets the pace. Can you pass the sacks on the beat without dropping one?

moor_ring.prompt: Find a mooring ring that is low enough to reach and strong enough to hold. Then loop the line the right way.

moor_wings.prompt: Wings carry the rope to a high ring. Can you pull the knot tight before the barge drifts?

delivery_sacks.narration: You form a line and pass the potato sacks onto the quay. The pilot lets his boat drift clear of the crooked steps. "Six crews eating tonight," he says. Then he digs under his seat and hands you a glass jar of glowing moss. "For the dark of the hold. It lights up when it's happy." He looks up at the landing. "Still need a new way home." The jar hums, very quietly, like a kettle with good manners.

sacks_dropped.narration: A sack bursts. Potatoes roll everywhere, bouncing off boots and plopping into the harbor. The whole line scrambles after them, and the pilot dives for the last one with his webbed feet. When the splashing stops, supper for six boats is ashore, though three potatoes have been swimming. "Six crews eating tonight," he says, wringing out his hat. "Mostly." He looks up at the landing. "Still need a new way home." One potato is never seen again. Everyone agrees it has gone somewhere nicer.

delivery_moor.narration: You guide the pilot toward a low mooring ring and help tie his boat beside the quay. He can carry the sacks ashore without jumping. "This will do for tonight," he says. He tosses a little carved charm into your hand. "For the river. It keeps your feet sure on wet boards." He looks up at the landing. "Tomorrow I have to find where my landing went." The charm is smooth and warm, and it smells a little like rain.

moor_drift.narration: The line slips off the ring, and the barge swings into the quay with a thump. Every potato sack hops. You grab the next mooring ring and tie it again, tighter this time, with everyone's thumbs on the knot. "This will do for tonight," the pilot says, patting his boat. He looks up at the landing. "Tomorrow I have to find where my landing went." Somewhere in the hull, a very small crab complains about the noise.

landing_steps.narration: The crooked steps hang off the wall above the water, tipped like a stair that fell asleep standing up. A thin, cold breath slips out from underneath them and smells of snow. "Whatever grabbed my landing, it didn't take it far," says the pilot. "I'd like it back by supper. Could somebody take a look?" It tickles your ankles like a cat that is not sure it likes you.

choices.label: Stack crates under the steps to hold them
Use smash to knock the steps straight

landing_climb.prompt: Grab the stone edge and haul yourself up. Can you hold on long enough to look underneath? The stone is wet, and the water below is a long way down and very cold.

landing_prop.prompt: Which crates are the right size? Stack them so the steps rest on something solid, and see what is hiding under there.

landing_smash.prompt: Smash can knock a stuck step back into place. Can you swing at the right spot without cracking the stone?

landing_clue.narration: Frost crusts the underside of the steps in neat white feathers. All of it points the same way, toward the far end of the quay, as if the stone were listening for something there. The pilot whistles through his teeth. "Well, I'll be a pond. Thank you." He flips you two coins for the trouble. It looks like a fern drawn by a very cold artist.

choices.label: Take the supper to the boats

landing_slip.narration: Your foot skids on a wet step, and the pilot catches your sleeve. You find nothing under there but a puddle and a very surprised snail. "Never mind," he says. "The steps lean toward the far end of the quay. Always have, since this morning. I was only hoping somebody could tell me why." The snail looks at you for a long moment, then goes back to its business.

choices.label: Take the supper to the boats

quay_rest.narration: The pilot calls a thank-you from his deck and tosses up a bag of warm potato skins. You sit on an upturned crate by the noodle stall to eat them. Behind the stalls, a ladder climbs the harbor master's house to the rooftops. From up there comes a lot of cawing, all of it on purpose. The skins are salty and perfect, and for a minute nobody mentions snow. The pilot asks whether anybody has ever eaten a potato skin on a day when the weather was going wrong. Nobody has. It is excellent.

choices.label: Climb the ladder to the rooftops

rookery.narration: You climb through a trapdoor onto the rooftops. Crows sit on every chimney pot and every gutter, and all of them are looking at you. A sign hangs on the tallest chimney: NO MESSING. (WITH US.) This rooftop school is called the Rookery. Here the crows train each Duskrunner, a hero who runs quick and quiet. They all teach at once. On a peg hangs a dusk hood, soft as a shadow. A Duskrunner's quickness lives in that hood, and a star circlet worn beside it only makes it itch. Someone has put a tiny doormat at the top of the ladder. "Wipe your feet," say the crows. "We don't get messed with up here. Anyone who wants the hood may try it on." Then, quieter: "Nobody who leaves the Exchange climbs our ladder again. Take the hood off somewhere far away, and you won't find us to put it back. So choose well."

variants.text: The crows of the Rookery eye you from every chimney pot. "Back again," they say, all at once. The sign still says NO MESSING. (WITH US.) The dusk hood waits on its peg for anyone who wants to try it on. You wipe your feet on the tiny doormat without being asked. "Remember," the crows say. "Once you leave the Exchange, our ladder is gone for you."

choices.label: Learn to cross the roof quietly

rookery_lesson.narration: The crows show you how to cross the roof without a sound. Step where the moss grows. Never on the loose tile. You hold your breath and cross. Nothing clatters, and nobody at the noodle stall looks up. Back at the ladder, you find a folded note in your pocket. Nobody saw it arrive. It says: "Saw that. Nice. Don't mess with us."

quay.narration: At the end of the quay, two stacks of crates lean toward a thin fold in the air. A loose rope slides across the wet boards. You can hear the harbor behind you, but from the fold comes only a deep, slow creak. A faint hum rises from the fold, like a held note that nobody is singing.

choices.label: Work out what is being pulled
Get people away from the crates
Use vanish to slip between the stacks
Set the mosslight jar down to show which way things lean

check_pattern.prompt: Can you spot which loose things will slide first?

onSuccess.narration: The rope, the barrel lid, the crates: everything leans toward the fold.

onFailure.narration: A barrel lid shoots past your ankle before you can point.

quay_slip.prompt: Vanish lets you melt into the shadows between the stacks. Can you see which loose things lean toward the fold before they start to slide?

quay_lit.narration: You set the jar on the boards, and the moss glows up bright and curious. Every long shadow in its light points the same way: the barrel lid, the rope, the crates, all toward the fold. You nudge a wedge under the nearest crate. The jar blinks twice, as if proud of itself, and one of the dock workers carries it off to light the rest of the quay. Beyond the crates, something small bleats.

pattern_seen.narration: You kick a wedge under the nearest crate and call a warning. The noodle seller catches her awning before it tears free. Beyond the crates, something small bleats. The wedge squeaks, proud and a little splintered.

pattern_missed.narration: The lid rolls upright, circles twice, and drops flat beside the fold. You pull everyone back from its path. Beyond the crates, something small bleats. The lid looks very pleased with its performance.

clear_check.prompt: Everyone spread out along the quay and wave people back from the crates. Shout, whistle, flap your hat, whatever it takes!

clear_quay.narration: You wave the market crowd back and lift the noodle awning clear of a sliding crate. The dock workers start passing buckets out of the way. Beyond the crates, something small bleats. A cat sits on a barrel and supervises.

clear_crowd.narration: The crowd does the opposite of leaving. Everyone leans in to see what the shouting is about, and a small boy sits on a barrel to watch. The dock workers have to shoo them back one by one, tutting. At last the quay is clear, and everyone is a little embarrassed. Beyond the crates, something small bleats.

crate_plan.narration: The nearest stack of crates groans and leans a finger's width closer to the fold. Two dock workers hang off its rope with their boots skidding on the wet boards. "We can't hold it!" one gasps. "Something heavy, or something clever, and quick!" Behind the stack, the small bleat comes again, a little weaker. If the crates slide, they will slide onto whatever is making that noise. Overhead, the gull shrieks that it saw this coming.

choices.label: Everyone grabs the rope and hauls
Wedge a plank under the stack
Blow the brave whistle to call more dock workers

crate_haul.prompt: Everyone grab the rope behind the dock workers! Dig in your heels and haul the stack back together on the count of three! The rope is wet and the crates are heavy, and the workers are very glad to see you.

crate_wedge.prompt: Which plank, and where? Wedge it under the stack at just the right spot, before the next groan.

whistle_call.narration: You blow the brave whistle. It is very, very loud. Pigeons leave the quay. Three shutters slam. Then a dozen dock workers come pounding down the boards from every direction, grab the rope and lean. The stack gives a long, sorry creak and stops. The whistle gives one last squeak and goes quiet for good.

crates_back.narration: The stack stops. The dock workers let go of the rope one finger at a time. One of them pats the top crate. "Good crate," she whispers. The wet boards still creak and the fold still breathes cold, but nothing else is sliding. Behind the stack, the small bleat comes again, closer now, and a little cross. The one who patted it looks as if she might offer it a cookie.

crates_slid.narration: The stack lurches. One crate tips off the top, slides to the edge of the fold and tips in. It does not land anywhere. It just goes, with a soft pop, and a cold puff comes back out. The dock workers stare. "Right," says one. "Nobody tell the crate's owner." The rest of the stack stops leaning, mostly because it has less to lean with. Behind it, the small bleat comes again, closer and a little cross.

gap.narration: Between the two stacks there is a narrow gap, and at the far end of it the air looks thin and wrinkled, like a curtain in a draft. The bleat comes from just beyond. You can squeeze through sideways, or climb over the lower stack and drop down. Neither is wide enough for a hurry. The frost on the stacks crackles like sugar.

gap_squeeze.prompt: Breathe in and slide through sideways without knocking a single crate. The stacks lean in on both sides to listen.

gap_climb.prompt: Find handholds on the lower stack and haul yourself over. Don't wobble it!

gap_through.narration: You come out the other side without knocking a single crate. The cold is stronger here, and the boards under your boots are wet with frost instead of water. A tuft of white fuzz sits on a nail. The bleat comes again, from right in front of you.

gap_scrape.narration: You scrape through with a squeak, and the crates grumble but hold. You lose a button and gain a splinter. The cold is stronger here, and the boards under your boots are wet with frost instead of water. A tuft of white fuzz sits on a nail. The bleat comes again, from right in front of you.

shimmer.narration: The fold opens. Cold, still air presses against your face, carrying the smell of very old ice. On the other side, snow lies under a white sky. Beside your boots stands a snowhorn goat kid, hardly taller than a bucket. It tries to climb your leg. A faint light traces its edge.

choices.label: Hold out some supper to tempt the kid
Get the kid away from the opening

kid_food.narration: You hold out a crust. The kid sniffs it, forgets everything else in the world, and trots straight to your boots. It gobbles the crust in three bites and leans against your shin, warm and sticky. Behind it, the fold ripples. Behind you, a mooring rope draws tight.

read_light.narration: Your Starweaver studies the light around the fold: Riftlight. The others watch a faint shimmer bend the air. The kid stamps twice, impatient to be picked up. Behind you, a mooring rope draws tight.

pull.narration: The rope snaps straight. Crates scrape over the boards. The kid skids toward the opening, all four hooves spread. A dock worker throws you a loose line. You have time to make one move.

choices.label: Swoop in with Skyward or Glide
Smash a crate into the path

variants.text: The crate you wedged is still holding. You have a clear space to plant your feet.
"You saved my fish. Let us save that little one," calls the seller. She catches the loose line and passes it over the crates, where you can reach it without stepping into their path.
The barge pilot catches the sliding potato sacks before they can strike your legs. Your path to the kid stays clear.
From his safely moored boat, the pilot calls, "Watch that crate on your left!" You see it tilt in time to step clear.

catch.prompt: Catch the kid before it reaches the fold.

onSuccess.narration: You scoop the kid up. Its hooves drum on your coat.

onFailure.narration: You catch a hoof, then the rest of the goat. A crate clips your shoulder.

anchor.prompt: Hold the line while everyone grabs on.

onSuccess.narration: You wrap the line around a mooring post. Everyone has a hand on it before the post gives.

onFailure.narration: The wet line slips. You grab the last loop, knock your knee, and pull the others with you.

swoop.prompt: Skyward or Glide lifts the kid. Can you keep the loose line clear of the sliding crates?

onSuccess.narration: Wings carry the kid clear of the crates. You guide the loose line past the wheels of a cart, keeping everyone together.

onFailure.narration: The line catches your foot and you bump your shoulder against a crate. Wings carry the kid clear anyway.

smash.prompt: Smash breaks a crate into a barrier. Can you guide the loose line around it?

onSuccess.narration: Wood cracks. You thread the line around the broken crate, buying time for everyone to hold on.

onFailure.narration: The broken crate skids away. The line pulls tight against your knee as you grab it.

brace.prompt: Brace holds the post steady. Can you keep the line taut while everyone gets a grip?

onSuccess.narration: The braced post holds. You take up the slack until every friend has the line. Then the boards lift.

onFailure.narration: The braced post holds, but the wet line slips through your hands and knocks you onto your knees.

caught.narration: You tuck the kid against your chest. The dock worker lets go of the line before it can take her too. Your friends grab hold of you. The quay folds out of sight.

together.narration: The kid scrambles into the loop of rope between you. You pull it close. The line holds your party together as the quay folds out of sight.

tumbled.narration: The kid lands against your chest. Someone catches your sleeve; someone else catches theirs. You tumble through together, dragging the loose end of the rope.

through.narration: For one breath there is no sound. Then your boots hit snow. You pull the kid inside your coat as the wind flings wet snow against your knees. It sneezes into your collar. Behind you the fold pinches shut, taking the harbor noise with it. A small pulse warms your hands, then waits there.

ridge_walk.narration: The wind pushes like a giant hand. You knot your coat into a sling around the kid, and everyone takes a corner. The low ridge is a few steps away. Keep the sling level, and the kid will not even notice the wind.

interaction.cue: Raise or lower your corner until the sling is level.
interaction.objectLabel: the kid in the coat sling

ridge_ok.narration: Linked together, you lean into the wind and walk. Each step is small and wobbly, but the wind has nothing to push against except all of you. The ridge grows larger. Behind it, the snow is quiet. The kid peeks out of your coat, sneezes, and looks very proud of itself.

ridge_drift.narration: The wind shoves, and you all slide sideways across the snow in a heap, like a toboggan with elbows. You stop against the low ridge, breathing hard and laughing a little. The kid peeks out of your coat, sneezes, and looks proud of you for whatever just happened.

ridge_lee.narration: Behind the ridge, the wind drops to a mutter. The snow here is deep and quiet, and the sky is the color of milk. The kid is shaking so hard its ears rattle. It needs warming before anything else.

options.label: Tuck it in your coat
options.reaction: The kid burrows into the warm wool and sighs.

options.label: Rub its cold hooves
options.reaction: The kid kicks its warming hooves and bleats happily.

options.label: Hum a quiet tune
options.reaction: The kid's ears twitch in time to the tune.

onSuccess.narration: The shaking stops. One small ear pokes out of your collar and listens to the wind.

onFailure.narration: The kid wiggles free, sneezes, and burrows back in on its own.

white.narration: White slopes rise around you. Far below, water runs under a skin of ice. The goat kid wriggles out of your coat, takes one look at the empty snowfield, and climbs straight back in. You gather in the shelter of the low ridge. Somewhere beyond it, a bell rings.

barge_toss.narration: The horn belongs to a supply barge, sliding toward the quay faster than a barge should. Its frogfolk pilot waves a boat hook in one hand. "Throw me the end of that rope!" he shouts. "Right over my hook, if you please!"

interaction.cue: Tap when the rope is over the pilot's hook.

onSuccess.narration: The rope drops neatly over his hook. "Lovely," says the pilot, and hauls the barge in.

onFailure.narration: The rope plops into the harbor. The pilot fishes it out with his hook, unbothered, and hauls the barge in.

sack_chain.narration: Six crews are waiting at their boats along the quay, and every one of them is hungry. The pilot sets a sack on the boards. "Pass them down the line, friend to friend," he says. "And mind the puddles. Potatoes hate puddles."

interaction.cue: Catch the sack, then pass it to the next friend.

onSuccess.narration: The sack sails from hand to hand without touching a puddle. Six crews cheer.

onFailure.narration: A sack lands in a puddle. A crew fishes it out, shakes it, and cheers anyway.

voiceGuide.tone: Warm, funny, curious, with real consequences. Describe actions and sensory details directly. Short dialogue. Never use "the kind of thing that", "the sort of thing that", or "it was X, the type of thing that makes you Y" comparisons. Let a character act instead of explaining how the reader should feel.
voiceGuide.vocabulary: Read aloud to an eight-year-old. Concrete words, short sentences, distinct voices.

npcVoices.Captain Thimble: Chapter-scoped kitsune Sky Island captain, practical and brisk. Frustrated with a displaced island, kind to helpers. No explanation for the displacement.
npcVoices.The gull: Indignant, literal, chilly. Brief complaints; never explains the magic.
npcVoices.Fish seller: Practical, protective of fish and helpers. Short dockside speech.
